Chapter 186

Opioids

Tintinalli Ch.186 — Section 15 Toxicology

Jennifer S. Love, Jeanmarie Perrone

🇹🇭 Thai EM Board📗 Rosen's⚕️ ATLS

Introduction and Epidemiology

Opioids refer broadly to all compounds related to opium that possess analgesic and sedative properties. Opiate describes the alkaloids codeine and morphine found naturally in the opium poppy plant, Papaver somniferum. Narcotic refers to a broader group of soporific drugs, a term predominantly used by law enforcement to refer to controlled substances with abuse or addictive potential; use of this term in medical practice is discouraged.

Opioid abuse is a significant public health issue in the United States with a dramatic increase in ED visits related to opioids in the past 20 years. Opioids were responsible for 66% of drug overdose deaths in the United States during 2016. The majority of prescription opioid overdose deaths were associated with diversion, doctor shopping, and nonmedical use.

Inline MCQ 3. Which is the most appropriate initial naloxone dose for an apneic adult with suspected chronic opioid use found unresponsive in the field?
A. 2 mg IV bolus
B. 0.04 mg IV
C. 0.4 mg IV
D. 4 mg IM
Answer: B. 0.04 mg IV is the recommended starting dose if the patient is breathing spontaneously and chronic use is suspected — minimizes precipitated withdrawal. Apneic patients warrant 2 mg per Tintinalli Table 186-3, but the question specified 'apneic with chronic use' — the safer initial titration is 0.04 mg followed by escalation. Refer to Table 186-3, Tintinalli p.1234.
Inline MCQ 4. Which of the following is NOT part of the classic opioid toxidrome triad?
A. Miosis
B. Respiratory depression
C. Hypertension
D. CNS depression
Answer: C. Triad = miosis + CNS depression + respiratory depression. Hypotension (not hypertension) may occur due to histamine release. Reference: Tintinalli Ch.186 p.1233.
Inline MCQ 5. A patient on long-term oxycodone is given 0.4 mg IV naloxone in the ED, then becomes severely agitated. The most likely explanation is:
A. Naloxone-induced anaphylaxis
B. Precipitated opioid withdrawal
C. Polypharmacy with stimulants
D. Serotonin syndrome
Answer: B. Precipitated withdrawal from too-rapid antagonism. Avoid by starting at 0.04 mg in chronic users. Tintinalli p.1234.
Inline MCQ 6. Which urine drug screen result would you NOT expect from a patient using only oxycodone?
A. Positive opiate immunoassay
B. Positive 6-MAM
C. Positive oxycodone-specific assay
D. Confirmation by GC/MS
Answer: B. Standard opiate immunoassays target morphine/codeine and may miss semisynthetics. 6-MAM (6-monoacetylmorphine) is specific for heroin metabolism, not oxycodone. Oxycodone requires a specific assay or GC/MS confirmation. Reference: Table 186-2, Tintinalli p.1234.
Inline MCQ 7. Which feature is MOST suggestive of methadone overdose specifically (vs. other opioids)?
A. Pinpoint pupils
B. QTc prolongation with torsades risk
C. Severe pruritus
D. Bradycardia
Answer: B. Methadone uniquely blocks hERG channels → QTc prolongation → torsades. Other opioids do not share this risk. Methadone's long half-life (12–18 h) also predisposes to delayed/recurrent toxicity. Tintinalli Ch.186.
Inline MCQ 8. An 8-h-old infant is born to a heroin-using mother. Which clinical feature would you EXPECT?
A. Excessive sleepiness only
B. Tremor, irritability, high-pitched cry, poor feeding (NAS)
C. Macrocephaly
D. Abdominal distention with ileus
Answer: B. Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS): autonomic hyperactivity (tremor, sweating, sneezing), CNS irritability (high-pitched cry, hypertonia, seizures), GI dysfunction (poor feeding, vomiting). Onset typically within 24–72 h. Reference: Tintinalli Ch.186, Special Populations.
Inline MCQ 9. Which feature differentiates fentanyl overdose from heroin overdose at presentation?
A. Miosis is absent in fentanyl
B. 'Wooden chest' rigidity from rapid IV push
C. Naloxone is ineffective for fentanyl
D. Withdrawal is more severe with fentanyl
Answer: B. Fentanyl can cause acute chest-wall rigidity from rapid IV bolus — characteristic but not specific. Heroin OD does not classically cause this. All opioids respond to naloxone but fentanyl analogues may need higher cumulative doses. Reference: Tintinalli Ch.186.
Inline MCQ 10. Which of the following is appropriate disposition for a patient who received 0.4 mg naloxone IV with full reversal at 30 min, now ambulating, with normal vitals — taking what was alleged to be 'just heroin'?
A. Discharge after 1 h observation
B. Observe at least 4 h (and longer if long-acting opioid suspected)
C. Admit to step-down for 24 h
D. Discharge AMA
Answer: B. Naloxone duration is 20-90 min. Heroin half-life is short, but methadone, sustained-release oxycodone, and fentanyl analogues outlast naloxone. Standard ED practice: ≥4-6 h observation; longer if exposure history is unclear. Reference: Tintinalli Disposition section.

Pharmacology

Opioids modulate nociception at the terminals of afferent nerves in the CNS, peripheral nervous system, and GI tract. Opioids are agonists at the three primary opioid receptors: μ (mu), κ (kappa), and δ (delta). Opioid receptors are similar to other G protein-coupled receptors; transmembrane proteins that undergo conformation change when activated by external molecules that then alters some aspect of intracellular function. Opioid receptors vary widely in morphology and distribution. In addition, the specificity and affinity of an opioid for a particular receptor are variable. For example, tramadol possesses 1/6000th the affinity of morphine at the μ-receptor site.

  • Stimulation of the μ-receptors results in analgesia, sedation, miosis, respiratory depression, cough suppression, euphoria, and decreased GI motility
  • Stimulation of κ-receptors results in weaker analgesia, sedation, miosis, decreased intestinal motility, dysphoria, and hallucinations
  • Stimulation of the δ-receptors results in some analgesia and antidepressant effect
  • All currently available opioid agonists possess μ-receptor activity and result in some degree of respiratory depression

Opioids can be categorized as naturally occurring compounds (termed opiates), chemical modifications of natural compounds (semisynthetic), and the synthetic derivatives. Some opioids are agonists at all opioid receptors (e.g., morphine and hydromorphone), whereas others are partial agonists–antagonists (e.g., pentazocine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, and buprenorphine) at the opioid receptors.

Opioids are readily absorbed, achieving peak blood levels 30 to 60 minutes after ingestion of standard oral formulations. But other pharmacokinetic elements can vary depending on whether the opioid is a short-acting, long-acting, or sustained-release formulation. Long-acting opioids, such as methadone, reach peak blood levels in 30 to 60 minutes, but have a long duration of effect and half-life. Sustained-release forms take longer to achieve peak blood levels; for example, morphine sulfate controlled-release tablets reach peak blood levels at 90 minutes compared with 30 minutes for standard morphine tablets.

After GI absorption, most opioids undergo first-pass hepatic metabolism, so bioavailability can vary from as low as 10% to as high as 80% after PO administration. Thus, at equal doses, most opioids are more potent given parenterally than PO. The opioids with good oral bioavailability are codeine, oxycodone, methadone, hydromorphone, and tapentadol.

The metabolism of codeine, meperidine, methadone, morphine, and oxycodone is primarily hepatic and subject to drug interactions and genetic variations. For example, antiretroviral medications can enhance the metabolism of methadone, which results in lower plasma methadone concentrations. As another example, codeine is metabolized to morphine via cytochrome P450 isoenzyme 2D6, an enzyme with genotypic and phenotypic variability. Patients with rapid cytochrome P450 enzyme 2D6 metabolism produce more morphine after a fixed dose of codeine.

In drug misuse, unconventional routes of administration (insufflating or injecting ground opioid tablets, heating fentanyl patches or applying multiple patches to the skin) may alter the drug's pharmacokinetics and often increase the rate of opioid absorption. Similarly, in opioid overdoses resulting in high plasma levels, the pharmacokinetics are altered due to enzymatic saturation. This may increase the severity of poisoning, delay the onset, and prolong the duration of action, as compared with the expected therapeutic actions.

Natural Opiates: Codeine (oral 200 mg ≈ morphine 10 mg SC), Morphine (oral 30 mg ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, half-life 2-4 h, duration 3-4 h). Semisynthetic: Buprenorphine (4 SL ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, partial agonist, duration 6-24 h, half-life 20-44 h), Hydrocodone (1.5 ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, duration 3-4 h), Hydromorphone (oral 7.5 ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, duration 3-4 h, half-life 2-3 h), Oxycodone (oral 20 ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, duration 3-6 h, half-life 3-4 h), Oxymorphone (6 ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, duration 4-6 h, half-life 7-11 h). Synthetic: Diphenoxylate (not available, 2.5 h duration), Fentanyl (0.125 mg ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, 0.1 mg parenteral dose, onset 1 min, duration 1 h, half-life 3-4 h), Meperidine (300 mg ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, 100 mg parenteral dose, duration 1-3 h, half-life 3-4 h for meperidine, 15-30 h for normeperidine metabolite), Methadone (20 mg ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, 10 mg parenteral dose, duration 8-12 h initially then 12-18 h chronically, half-life 12-18 h or up to 59 h with chronic use), Tapentadol (75 mg ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, duration 4-6 h, half-life 4-5 h), Tramadol (100 mg ≈ morphine 10 mg SC, duration 4-6 h, half-life 5-7 h)

Clinical Features of Opioid Intoxication

The brief descriptor of the widely recognized opioid toxidrome would include the triad of miosis, lethargy, and respiratory depression. The full effects associated with opioid intoxication also can include orthostatic hypotension, nausea and vomiting (especially in opioid-naive patients), histamine release resulting in localized urticaria, bronchospasm, ileus secondary to decreased GI motility, and urinary retention secondary to increased vesical sphincter tone. The depression in mental status can be profound.

The respiratory depression is characterized by slow and shallow respirations that can produce hypercarbia, hypoxia, and cyanosis. Miosis is not universally present from intoxication with every opioid; normal or even enlarged pupils have been documented secondary to pentazocine and meperidine toxicity. Mydriasis may also signal severe cerebral hypoxia or result from co-ingestants (diphenoxylate, heroin, scopolamine).

Other possible findings in opioid toxicity include hypothermia, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome, myoglobinuric renal failure, and seizures associated with overdoses of tramadol and meperidine.

Opioid-induced acute lung injury, previously known as noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, is an uncommon complication associated with opioid overdose. Acute lung injury can occur immediately or be delayed up to 24 hours after overdose and presents with tachypnea, rales, decreased oxygen saturation, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with a normal cardiac silhouette on chest radiograph. The incidence of acute lung injury is 10% in patients with severe overdose requiring naloxone.

The pathophysiology of opioid-induced acute lung injury is poorly understood and may be multifactorial. Pulmonary edema may result from direct alveolar injury from hypoxia, opioid-induced histamine release, capillary leak due to negative inspiratory pressure, or neurogenic injury. Treatment includes oxygen supplementation and ventilatory support, with either noninvasive or invasive modalities. Additional naloxone, diuretics, and digoxin are not indicated.

The combination of meperidine, tramadol, or dextromethorphan with monoamine oxidase inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or linezolid can result in serotonin syndrome. Serotonin syndrome is characterized by a spectrum of altered mentation from anxiety to delirium, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, hyperreflexia, and muscle rigidity, especially in the lower extremities. Although uncommon, deaths have been reported. Naloxone is not effective in treating opioid-induced serotonin syndrome.

Diagnosis

The triad of lethargy, miosis, and respiratory depression strongly suggests opioid intoxication, and in many clinical scenarios, specific evidence of opioid use is present. The combination of a respiratory rate of <12 breaths/min, miosis, and circumstantial evidence of opioid use (drug paraphernalia, needle marks, presence of a tourniquet, bystander corroboration) was highly sensitive for opioid overdose in the prehospital setting.

Physical examination should be thorough: patients should be undressed completely yet carefully because drug use paraphernalia including needles and syringes may be hidden within clothing. Look for evidence of injection drug use, concealed opioids, or fentanyl patches on all parts of the body, including mucous cavities. Listen for auscultatory findings suggestive of pulmonary edema; palpate muscle groups to detect signs of compartment syndrome.

The differential diagnosis of opioid intoxication includes toxicologic exposure to drugs and compounds that produce similar findings, such as clonidine, organophosphates and carbamates, phenothiazines and atypical antipsychotic medications, sedative-hypnotic medications, and carbon monoxide. Clonidine overdoses are characterized by coma, bradycardia, hypotension, miosis, and periods of apnea that respond to tactile or auditory stimulation. Organophosphate and carbamate overdoses cause the cholinergic toxidrome: miosis, muscle fasciculations, profuse vomiting and diarrhea, and sweating. Phenothiazines, olanzapine, and risperidone cause neurologic depression and miosis from decreased adrenergic tone. Gamma-hydroxybutyrate intoxication is associated with profound CNS depression, bradypnea, and, occasionally, miosis. Sedative-hypnotic agents and carbon monoxide cause profound neurologic depression but are not usually associated with miosis. Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, CNS infections, postictal states, and pontine and intracranial hemorrhages should also be considered in the differential diagnosis.

A qualitative urine opioid screen may aid in the diagnosis, but available tests have limitations. The assay in most commercially available urine opioid screens recognizes morphine. Opioids that are metabolized to morphine, such as codeine and heroin, as well as hydromorphone are detected by this urine assay as opiates. Specific immunoassay screens are available for oxycodone, fentanyl, or methadone. Confirmation of a positive immunoassay screen requires gas chromatography/mass spectroscopy testing. Some common medications will produce false-positive results on opioid drug screens.

A urine opioid screen can be positive up to 2 to 4 days after a single use of codeine, morphine, or heroin. The oxycodone, fentanyl, and methadone-specific screens can be positive up to 3 days after ingestion. As with most urine drug screening in the ED, detection of a drug taken in the recent past may not correctly identify the toxicologic cause of the patient's current condition. Serum acetaminophen concentration should be obtained in all suicidal ingestions and all cases of combination opioid–acetaminophen ingestions.

Standard urine opioid screens detect morphine, codeine, and heroin metabolites but NOT fentanyl, methadone, buprenorphine, tramadol, or novel synthetic opioids. Specific immunoassay screens required for these agents. False-positives reported with chlorpromazine, clomipramine, diphenhydramine, doxylamine, ibuprofen, quetiapine, thioridazine, verapamil, poppy seeds, and rifampin. Clinical diagnosis (respiratory depression + miosis + altered mental status) often more reliable than urine screens.

Management

Airway protection and ventilatory assistance are the most important treatment steps for opioid intoxications, because respiratory depression is the major morbidity and the cause of mortality. Use bag-valve mask ventilatory support as needed to initially maintain adequate oxygenation and ventilation. After adequate ventilation is ensured, administer naloxone. Endotracheal intubation may be necessary in some cases of opioid or polysubstance overdose with respiratory depression unresponsive or poorly responsive to naloxone or in cases in which acute lung injury is suspected. Intubation offers the advantages of airway protection, easy access for suctioning, and provision of an alternate route of administration for some medications.

Single-dose activated charcoal (1 gram/kg PO) may be indicated in some patient populations, such as pediatric oral ingestion, if the patient is fully awake, or after the airway is protected with an endotracheal tube. Under special circumstances, delayed and multiple doses of activated charcoal may be useful, as in diphenoxylate hydrochloride–atropine sulfate overdoses and in cases of large ingestions of sustained-release preparations.

Naloxone, a derivative of oxymorphone, is a pure competitive antagonist at all opioid receptors, with particular affinity for μ-receptors. Therefore, naloxone fully reverses all the effects of opioids, including respiratory depression, sedation, miosis, and analgesia. The elimination half-life of naloxone is 60 to 90 minutes, but the duration of action is as short as 20 minutes if a large amount of opioid agonist is present.

Naloxone has poor oral bioavailability but is well absorbed when given by injection (IV, SC, or IM), inhaled, or deposited on mucosa (intratracheally or intranasally, but not sublingual). Inhaled naloxone by nebulization is reasonably effective in reversing depressed mental status and respirations in opioid toxicity, with about 10% requiring additional rescue parenteral naloxone. Intranasally administered naloxone provides a pharmacokinetic profile similar to that of IM or SC naloxone and is used by EMS personnel and in bystander naloxone administration programs.

Naloxone effectiveness is dependent on the dose administered and the amount of opioid that needs to be reversed, balanced against the risk of precipitating withdrawal. There is wide variation in recommended naloxone doses to treat opioid toxicity. It is prudent to use a small starting dose of naloxone, 0.04 milligram IV, in opioid-dependent patients who present with mental status depression and modest respiratory depression, because larger doses can induce opioid withdrawal symptoms in these individuals. An initial dose of naloxone, 0.4 milligram IV, is recommended in non–opioid-dependent patients who present with mental status depression and modest respiratory depression. Subsequent doses of naloxone of 0.04 milligram to 0.4 milligram IV are administered every 2 to 3 minutes until the desired effect is reached. Incremental dosing of naloxone mitigates the precipitation of acute opioid withdrawal.

For patients presenting with apnea or near-apnea and cyanosis, a large starting dose of naloxone, 2 milligrams IV, should be administered regardless of drug use history. Repeated doses of 2 milligrams IV every 3 minutes are recommended until a maximum of 10 milligrams IV is reached or respiratory depression is reversed. Exposures to fentanyl, novel synthetic opioids, and sustained-release preparations may require these larger-than-ordinary doses. Toxicity from leaking opioid-containing packets in the intestinal tract (i.e., in "body packers") can be extremely severe, and such patients require large and sustained naloxone doses until the drug-containing packets are expelled or removed.

The duration of action of naloxone may be shorter than that of the offending opioid, so naloxone infusions are occasionally required to support respiration over several hours as the opioid is metabolized. This is especially true for certain long-acting opioids, such as buprenorphine and methadone; for exposures to sustained-release preparations; and for ingestions of transdermal fentanyl patches. A continuous infusion should be considered only if the patient responded to the initial naloxone bolus and subsequently required repeat administration. To calculate the naloxone continuous infusion dose, determine the "wake-up dose" and administer two thirds of that dose per hour by IV infusion. Adjustments may be required if the patient develops respiratory depression (by repeating a bolus and increasing infusion rates) or withdrawal symptoms (by decreasing infusion rates). It is recommended that patients on naloxone infusions be admitted to a monitored unit.

Naloxone has a remarkable safety profile. When administered to opioid-naive patients, naloxone has no adverse effects. Although adverse effects are seen in about one third of patients who receive it for a suspected opioid overdose, serious complications are rare. The most common adverse effects associated with naloxone are anxiety, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, piloerection, yawning, and rhinorrhea, which are expected signs and symptoms of opioid withdrawal. Careful dosing of naloxone can prevent the precipitation of opioid withdrawal symptoms.

IV: Chronic opioid users with modest respiratory depression: 0.04 mg; opioid-naive with modest respiratory depression: 0.4 mg; apneic or cyanotic (any history): 2 mg. Subsequent doses: 0.04–0.4 mg IV every 2–3 minutes until desired effect (max 10 mg). IM/SC: 2 mg. Intranasal: 2 mg (1 mg per nostril). Nebulized: 2 mg in 3 mL saline. Onset: IV 1–2 min, IM/SC 5–6 min, intranasal/nebulized 6–8 min. Duration: 20–90 minutes (shorter with large opioid amounts). For long-acting opioids: Calculate naloxone infusion at 2/3 of wake-up dose per hour.

Special Populations and Specific Opioids

Buprenorphine is a mixed opioid agonist–antagonist, with partial agonist activity at μ-receptors and antagonist activity at κ- and δ-receptors. Because buprenorphine is only a partial agonist at μ-receptors, it has decreased intrinsic activity that causes its clinical effects to plateau at higher dosages. Buprenorphine has high affinity for and slow dissociation from the μ-receptor, which results in a long duration of action. Furthermore, other opioid agonists (such as heroin) or antagonists (such as naloxone) cannot easily displace buprenorphine from the μ-receptor. Buprenorphine has poor oral bioavailability because of extensive first-pass metabolism and is therefore administered using sublingual films or tablets or parenterally. The most frequently prescribed sublingual buprenorphine formulation is in combination with naloxone in a 4:1 ratio. Because naloxone has poor bioavailability from PO or sublingual administration, it was introduced into the preparation to discourage and limit parenteral abuse of the buprenorphine portion while not interfering with therapeutic use in the form of the sublingual film.

Buprenorphine can be associated with three distinct clinical scenarios. First, the opioid-naive patient who overdoses on buprenorphine will experience mental status depression, nausea, vomiting, miosis, and respiratory depression (usually with a plateau). In this situation, low-dose naloxone may not be fully effective in reversing mental status and respiratory depression. Because of the long duration of action of buprenorphine, naloxone infusions are necessary, and admission to the hospital is necessary in symptomatic patients. The second possible scenario is buprenorphine exposure in the opioid-dependent patient. In this case, buprenorphine will precipitate opioid withdrawal symptoms, because the partial agonist buprenorphine behaves like an antagonist in the presence of an agonist. Buprenorphine-induced withdrawal is best managed with symptom-driven therapy, including antiemetics, nonopioid analgesics, antidiarrheal medications, and nonbenzodiazepine sedatives. The third possible clinical scenario is buprenorphine exposure in the opioid-dependent patient who is suffering from opioid withdrawal, in whom buprenorphine will act as a partial agonist and alleviate the symptoms of opioid withdrawal. Thus, buprenorphine is unique in that it can both induce and treat opioid withdrawal, depending on the timing of its administration. Buprenorphine can be used in the ED to alleviate opioid withdrawal and be prescribed upon ED discharge to transition patients with opioid use disorder to medication-assisted treatment.

Methadone is a synthetic opioid used as opioid replacement therapy in opioid dependence and can be prescribed as an analgesic for chronic pain. The initial analgesic duration is 8 to 12 hours with an elimination half-life of 12 to 18 hours. With repetitive dosing, analgesic action duration and elimination half-life increase to approximately 22 to 36 hours and up to 59 hours, respectively. The long duration of activity enables once-a-day dosing during chronic therapy. Methadone has a higher risk for overdose-related deaths than other opioids, often with co-ingestants. Acute methadone overdoses present similarly to other opioid intoxications, but the duration can be much longer, requiring naloxone infusions with close neurologic and respiratory monitoring.

Methadone has several drug–drug interactions that can precipitate toxicity or withdrawal in patients on chronic therapy. Interactions between methadone and human immunodeficiency virus medications are common and complex, creating potential for both increased toxicity and withdrawal. The relevant interactions for emergency physicians include ciprofloxacin, fluconazole, ketoconazole, and omeprazole, which can increase toxicity. Drug–methadone interactions that have potential to precipitate withdrawal include macrolides (especially clarithromycin), phenobarbital, phenytoin, spironolactone, and verapamil.

Methadone prolongs the QT interval in acute overdose or during long-term methadone treatment, providing the potential for cardiac dysrhythmias, such as torsades de pointes. In patients with acute methadone overdose resulting in QT interval prolongation, serum electrolytes should be optimized and the patient should be admitted to a monitored unit until the condition resolves. Patients on long-term methadone therapy who develop a QTc interval between 450 and 500 milliseconds do not require a dosage adjustment, but electrolyte imbalances should be corrected if present, and patients should be followed on an outpatient basis with frequent ECGs. Patients who develop a QTc interval of >500 milliseconds should be considered for methadone dosage reduction or discontinuation.

Tramadol is being increasingly prescribed in the United States for chronic pain. Tramadol binds norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake inhibitors to contribute to its analgesic effects. Tramadol has no direct opiate-binding capacity, but after it is metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes, the active metabolite, O-desmethyltramadol, binds the μ-opioid receptor. Tramadol's opioid effects can vary widely because of genetic variation, liver disease, renal disease, and co-prescribed drugs that affect cytochrome P450 metabolism capacity.

Tramadol overdoses are associated with lethargy, nausea, tachycardia, and seizures. At doses exceeding 500 milligrams, coma, hypertension, respiratory depression, and apnea are seen. Features consistent with serotonin syndrome have been seen in isolated tramadol overdoses. Tramadol-induced seizures are common, and naloxone is ineffective in preventing them. Fortunately, tramadol-induced seizures are usually single, and anticonvulsants are not necessary. Tramadol has also been associated with higher rates of hypoglycemia compared to codeine, especially within the first 30 days of use. Dependence during chronic therapy and withdrawal symptoms upon discontinuation have been reported with tramadol.

The mixed agonists–antagonists include pentazocine, butorphanol, and nalbuphine. These agents have variable but mostly antagonist activity at the μ-receptor and agonist effects at the κ-receptor. They may cause significant respiratory depression in overdose, and naloxone will reverse this respiratory depression. Mixed agonists–antagonists usually precipitate withdrawal when taken by an opioid-dependent individual, which reduces their potential for abuse. Pentazocine overdose can cause seizures.

Diphenoxylate hydrochloride–atropine sulfate is a frequently prescribed antidiarrheal agent. The medication is formulated as a combination tablet or liquid, containing diphenoxylate, 2.5 milligrams, and atropine, 0.025 milligram, in each tablet or 5 mL of liquid. In an overdose, initially the anticholinergic toxidrome dominates the clinical picture. The second phase of intoxication is characterized by the opioid toxidrome. Children <6 years of age can be symptomatic after ingestion of a single tablet. In pediatric patients, absorption can be delayed up to 6 to 12 hours in some cases because of the effect of atropine on GI motility. Admission and observation for 24 hours are recommended for children <6 years of age after ingestion of a combination tablet of diphenoxylate and atropine. Older children and adults should be observed in the ED for 6 hours. Administration of activated charcoal is recommended unless contraindicated.

Fentanyl and novel synthetic opioids have contributed to rising opioid overdose deaths since 2016. Novel synthetic opioids include both fentanyl analogs (acetylfentanyl, butyrlfentanyl, furanylfentanyl, carfentanil) and nonfentanyl μ-opioid agonists (U47700), all with varying and usually high potencies. Illicitly manufactured fentanyl is 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine and has been detected in >50% of opioid overdose deaths in some states. Illicitly manufactured fentanyl has been found as a contaminant in opioids, benzodiazepines, and cocaine. Due to their ultrapotency, overdoses of illicitly manufactured fentanyl and novel synthetic opioids may require rapidly escalating and higher doses of naloxone, up to 10 to 20 milligrams IV, to reverse respiratory depression related to overdose.

Heroin is often mixed with other compounds, such as cocaine, scopolamine, clenbuterol, and fentanyl, which may contribute to varied opioid toxidromes. Adulterants found in illicit heroin may include strychnine, quinine, lactose, and talc. Scopolamine is an antimuscarinic agent that produces the anticholinergic toxidrome. Clenbuterol is a long-acting β-adrenergic agonist similar to albuterol and is used in veterinary medicine. A potent neurotoxin, 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3-tetrahydropyridine, has been used as a meperidine adulterant, producing parkinsonism in users.

Starting in Russia in 2010, episodes of deaths and gangrene were reported associated with IV desomorphine or "Krokodil," a synthetic alternative to heroin crudely made from codeine tablets with a high concentration of tissue-toxic impurities. The colloquial name is derived from the appearance of the skin after it is injected.

Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) has mitragynine as its principal alkaloid, with stimulating effects at low doses (cocaine-like effect) and sedative effects (opioid-like effect) at high doses. Kratom has been used since the early 1930s in Africa and Southeast Asia for medicinal purposes and more recently to prevent opioid withdrawal symptoms by smoking, consuming, brewing, or mixing into drinks. There has been growing use of kratom in Western countries due to its availability in smoke shops and on the Internet. Since 2010, there has been a 10-fold increase in reported use in the United States.

Kratom is used in the United States for three distinct indications: (1) to help manage chronic pain, (2) to mitigate withdrawal symptoms from opioids or alcohol, and (3) for acute euphoric effects. Daily kratom use can lead to dependence, craving, and withdrawal symptoms. Kratom can produce seizures, serious toxicity, or even death, often associated with other drug use, such as decongestants, antidepressants, and benzodiazepines. Krypton, a combination containing kratom, O-desmethyltramadol, and caffeine, has also been associated with fatalities.

Loperamide, also known as "the poor man's methadone," has seen rising rates of misuse, abuse, and suicide ingestion since 2010. At high doses (between 50 and 300 milligrams, 20 to 150 times the therapeutic dose of 2 milligrams), loperamide binds the μ-opioid receptor and has greater CNS penetration, leading to euphoria and mental depression. It can also cause severe cardiotoxic effects, including QTc prolongation, QRS widening, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and other cardiac dysrhythmias, due to both sodium and potassium channel blockade.

Treatment of loperamide overdose should target three modes: GI decontamination, respiratory depression, and cardiotoxicity. Activated charcoal may be used for GI decontamination and repeated because loperamide inhibits peristalsis. Standard doses of naloxone (0.04 to 0.4 milligram) should be used to reverse respiratory depression. Cardiotoxicity due to sodium channel blockade potential with widened QRS complex is treated with sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mEq/kg IV, along with potassium and magnesium replacement. For patients with torsades de pointes, case reports have demonstrated success with cardiac overdrive pacing and isoproterenol IV infusions at 2 to 10 micrograms/min. Other advanced therapies including intravenous lipid emulsion therapy and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation have had limited success in individual cases.

Opioid Withdrawal

Downregulation of endogenous endorphins, dynorphins, and opioid receptors occurs with long-term use of opioids. Abrupt cessation of opioid use does not allow time for upregulation of receptors and results in increased neuronal firing and the opioid withdrawal syndrome. Opioid withdrawal typically starts 6 to 12 hours after last use of short-acting opioids and 30 hours after abstinence from long-acting opioids.

Opioid withdrawal can be abruptly precipitated by the administration of antagonists such as naloxone or naltrexone or the administration of partial agonist–antagonists such as buprenorphine. Opioid withdrawal usually starts with anxiety and progresses with development of additional symptoms over the next 12 to 24 hours. Opioid withdrawal symptoms usually peak on the third day of abstinence and resolve by the fifth or sixth day. Opioid withdrawal symptoms are very uncomfortable but are not life-threatening and rarely fatal. Vomiting and aspiration of gastric contents can cause pneumonitis and dehydration.

  • Initial features (6-12 hours post-short-acting opioid): anxiety, yawning, drug craving, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, diaphoresis, myalgias
  • Additional features (12-24 hours): irritability, tremor, piloerection, mydriasis
  • Subsequent features: insomnia, muscle spasms, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
  • Peak effects: 36-72 hours for short-acting opioids; symptoms resolve by day 5-6
  • Important: Withdrawal is NOT life-threatening but VERY uncomfortable; treatment is symptom-driven

Clinical scoring tools have been developed to assist in the assessment of opioid withdrawal. The commonly used Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) calculates a score based on the severity of 11 symptoms and can be used to assess appropriateness for buprenorphine or methadone and to monitor response to treatment. Scoring: 5-12 = mild; 13-24 = moderate; 25-36 = moderately severe; >36 = severe withdrawal.

Resting pulse rate, sweating, restlessness, pupil size, bone/joint aches, runny nose/tearing, GI upset, tremor, yawning, anxiety/irritability, gooseflesh skin. Total score sum of all 11 items. Used to assess timing of buprenorphine therapy and monitor treatment response.

Disposition and Follow-up

The optimal observation period after an opioid intoxication is determined by the history and clinical picture. Patients with presumed heroin intoxication who respond to naloxone can be safely discharged 1 hour after administration of naloxone if they have independent mobility, normal vital signs, and normal mental status.

In cases of exposure to opioids other than heroin, an observation period of 4 to 6 hours in the ED is recommended after the last naloxone administration. In long-acting opioid overdose, observation should be extended for a minimum of 8 hours. Moderate to severely symptomatic patients usually require hospital admission to monitored settings and may require continued administration of naloxone. A behavioral health evaluation is needed in cases with suicidal intent.

Heroin: 1 hour post-naloxone (if responsive, stable vitals, normal mentation). Other opioids: 4-6 hours post-last naloxone. Long-acting opioids (methadone, buprenorphine, sustained-release): minimum 8 hours. Patients on naloxone infusions: admit to monitored unit. Suicidal overdose: behavioral health evaluation before discharge.

⚕️ ATLS 11th Edition — Initial Assessment

📗 Rosen's EM 10th — Poisoned Patient Management

Key Pearls

Opioid toxidrome: Classic triad of miosis (pinpoint pupils), lethargy (altered mental status), and respiratory depression. Respiratory depression is the PRIMARY CAUSE OF MORTALITY. Airway protection and ventilation are the FIRST interventions, BEFORE naloxone.
Receptor pharmacology: μ-receptors cause analgesia, miosis, respiratory depression, euphoria, decreased GI motility; κ-receptors cause weaker analgesia and dysphoria; δ-receptors contribute some analgesia. All clinically available opioids have μ-activity and cause respiratory depression.
Pharmacokinetics vary widely: Short-acting opioids (heroin, immediate-release morphine) peak 30-60 min, duration 2-4 hours; long-acting opioids (methadone, buprenorphine) have duration 8-24 hours and half-lives up to 59 hours. Oral bioavailability ranges 10-80% due to first-pass metabolism; parenteral forms more potent.
Naloxone is a pure competitive μ-antagonist with half-life 60-90 minutes but DURATION AS SHORT AS 20 MINUTES with large opioid agonist present. This creates significant RE-SEDATION RISK, necessitating observation and naloxone infusions for long-acting opioids.
Naloxone dosing by clinical presentation: Chronic users with modest depression: 0.04 mg IV (prevents acute withdrawal); opioid-naive with modest depression: 0.4 mg IV; apneic/cyanotic (any history): 2 mg IV regardless of use. Titrate incremental doses 0.04-0.4 mg every 2-3 minutes. Fentanyl/novel synthetic opioids may require 10-20 mg IV.
Naloxone infusions essential for long-acting opioids and sustained-release preparations. Calculate infusion as 2/3 of 'wake-up dose' per hour IV. Adjust for respiratory depression (increase rate, repeat bolus) or withdrawal (decrease rate). Admission to monitored unit mandatory.
Buprenorphine: Partial μ-agonist with HIGH AFFINITY and SLOW DISSOCIATION from receptors. Standard naloxone doses may be ineffective; may require naloxone infusions even in opioid-naive overdose. Unique property: can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients OR alleviate withdrawal in withdrawing patients depending on timing.
Fentanyl and novel synthetic opioids (acetylfentanyl, carfentanil) are 50-100× more potent than morphine. Increasingly found as illicit heroin adulterant/contaminant. Require escalating naloxone doses (up to 10-20 mg IV) for reversal. Rising cause of overdose deaths.
Acute lung injury (noncardiogenic pulmonary edema): Occurs in ~10% severe overdoses, can be delayed up to 24 hours. Presents tachypnea, rales, hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates with normal cardiac silhouette. Treatment: oxygen and ventilatory support only; naloxone, diuretics, digoxin NOT indicated.
Opioid withdrawal: Begins 6-12 hours post-short-acting, 30 hours post-long-acting; peaks day 3; resolves day 5-6. Symptoms: mydriasis, tachycardia, insomnia, anxiety, myalgias, nausea, vomiting. UNCOMFORTABLE BUT NOT LIFE-THREATENING. Managed symptomatically (antiemetics, nonopioid analgesics, antidiarrheal, sedatives); buprenorphine can be used acutely to alleviate withdrawal.
Observation periods: Heroin 1 hour post-naloxone (if stable); other opioids 4-6 hours; long-acting opioids 8+ hours minimum. Loperamide ('poor man's methadone'): causes opioid effects AND severe cardiotoxicity (QT prolongation, QRS widening) requiring sodium bicarbonate, electrolyte correction, and possible overdrive pacing. Tramadol: causes seizures (naloxone-resistant)—anticonvulsants may be needed despite naloxone administration.

Inline Assessment MCQs

Q1. A 28-year-old male with a history of heroin use is found unresponsive in an alley with a respiratory rate of 6 breaths/min, pinpoint pupils, and no air movement on auscultation. EMS personnel have initiated bag-valve-mask ventilation. What is the next appropriate step?
  • A. Continue bag-valve-mask ventilation; await blood gas results before administering naloxone
  • B. Administer naloxone 0.04 mg IV to avoid precipitating severe acute withdrawal
  • C. Intubate for airway protection; naloxone can be given after intubation if needed
  • D. Administer naloxone 2 mg IV immediately while continuing bag-valve-mask ventilation
❌ Incorrect. While bag-valve-mask is essential, naloxone should not be delayed. Respiratory depression is the cause of mortality; naloxone must be given immediately after adequate ventilation is ensured.
❌ Incorrect. While low-dose naloxone (0.04 mg) is appropriate for chronic users with modest respiratory depression, this patient is apneic and critically ill. High-dose naloxone (2 mg) is indicated for apnea/cyanosis regardless of use history. Severe withdrawal is preferable to death.
❌ Incorrect. Naloxone should not be delayed while preparing for intubation. Naloxone can reverse the opioid effect within minutes, often avoiding the need for intubation. It should be given as soon as ventilation is adequate.
✅ Correct. High-dose naloxone (2 mg IV) is indicated for apnea/cyanosis. IV route has fastest onset (1–2 minutes). Bag-valve-mask ventilation should continue simultaneously to ensure oxygenation.
Q2. A 34-year-old female with chronic pain on methadone maintenance therapy presents 4 hours after intentional overdose of her methadone supply. She responds to naloxone 2 mg IV with return of spontaneous respirations and arousal. However, 30 minutes later, she becomes lethargic and has respiratory depression (RR 8) again despite continued observation. What is the most appropriate management?
  • A. Administer another naloxone bolus 2 mg IV and discharge after 1 hour observation
  • B. Administer activated charcoal to reduce methadone absorption
  • C. Calculate and initiate a continuous naloxone infusion at two-thirds of the wake-up dose per hour; admit to monitored unit
  • D. Intubate and mechanically ventilate until methadone is metabolized (24–48 hours); avoid naloxone infusion
❌ Incorrect. Another bolus will provide only temporary reversal; re-sedation will recur after 20–90 minutes when naloxone is metabolized. Methadone's long duration requires naloxone infusion, not repeated boluses. Discharge is inappropriate for methadone overdose.
❌ Incorrect. Activated charcoal is not indicated for parenteral opioid toxicity and will not reverse already-absorbed methadone. Naloxone is the treatment of choice.
✅ Correct. Methadone's long duration of action necessitates naloxone infusion rather than repeated boluses. The infusion dose prevents re-sedation and maintains reversal. This patient requires ICU or high-acuity admission with continuous monitoring.
❌ Incorrect. While intubation may be necessary if naloxone infusion cannot maintain adequate respiration, naloxone infusion should be attempted first. It is effective in preventing re-sedation and avoiding prolonged ventilation.

Thai EM Board MCQs

Q1. Which of the following clinical scenarios is most consistent with opioid withdrawal rather than opioid intoxication?
  • A. Pinpoint pupils, lethargy, respiratory depression, bradycardia 2 hours after heroin ingestion
  • B. Dilated pupils, insomnia, tachycardia, anxiety, body aches 48 hours after last opioid use
  • C. Miosis, nausea, vomiting, ileus, hypotension
  • D. Seizures, hyperthermia, autonomic instability within 6 hours of opioid cessation
❌ Incorrect. This is classic opioid intoxication (miosis, CNS depression, respiratory depression). Opioid withdrawal is not this acute.
✅ Correct. This is typical opioid withdrawal. Mydriasis (dilated pupils), hyperarousal (insomnia, anxiety), tachycardia, and myalgias are hallmarks. Timeline (48 hours post-cessation) fits short-acting opioid withdrawal.
❌ Incorrect. This is opioid intoxication (miosis, nausea, ileus). Withdrawal causes mydriasis and hyperactivity.
❌ Incorrect. Opioid withdrawal begins at 6–12 hours for short-acting opioids and peaks 36–72 hours. While autonomic instability occurs, seizures and hyperthermia (at 6 hours) are atypical for opioid withdrawal and suggest another etiology (stimulant withdrawal, serotonin syndrome, sepsis).
Q2. A 31-year-old male with no prior medical history presents to the ED with chest pain, palpitations, and altered mental status after ingesting 75 tablets of loperamide (total 150 mg) in a suicide attempt. ECG shows prolonged QT interval. What is the PRIMARY mechanism of loperamide toxicity in this case?
  • A. High-dose loperamide causes opioid-like effects (CNS depression) AND sodium/potassium channel blockade causing QT prolongation and cardiac dysrhythmias
  • B. Loperamide directly inhibits cardiac potassium channels; μ-opioid receptors are not involved in overdose toxicity
  • C. QT prolongation from loperamide is mediated via μ-opioid receptors in cardiac tissue
  • D. Loperamide causes QT prolongation only in patients with underlying cardiac disease or electrolyte abnormalities
✅ Correct. Loperamide's cardiovascular toxicity is its most dangerous feature at high doses. The prolonged QT is from sodium/potassium channel effects, not opioid receptors. Both opioid and cardiac mechanisms contribute to lethality.
❌ Incorrect. Loperamide does block sodium and potassium channels (explaining QT prolongation), but it also binds μ-opioid receptors at high doses, contributing to CNS depression and respiratory depression. Both mechanisms are important.
❌ Incorrect. The QT prolongation is from direct sodium/potassium channel blockade, not μ-opioid receptor activation. While loperamide has opioid effects at high doses, the cardiotoxicity is channel-mediated.
❌ Incorrect. High-dose loperamide can cause QT prolongation and dysrhythmias in previously healthy individuals. While baseline risk factors may increase susceptibility, loperamide's cardiotoxicity is dose-dependent, not contingent on pre-existing disease.
Q3. A 42-year-old male with a history of opioid use disorder is found unresponsive with respiratory depression. He is administered naloxone 0.4 mg IV. Within 2 minutes, he becomes alert with normal respirations (RR 14). However, 15 minutes later, he becomes combative, complains of severe body aches and cramping, and demands more opioids. What is occurring?
  • A. Allergic reaction to naloxone; discontinue immediately and administer antihistamines
  • B. Inadequate naloxone dosing; administer another 0.4 mg IV bolus
  • C. Stimulant contamination of the original opioid; patient is likely experiencing cocaine/methamphetamine intoxication
  • D. Acute opioid withdrawal precipitated by naloxone antagonism; withdraw causes dysphoria, body aches, insomnia, and drug craving but is NOT life-threatening
❌ Incorrect. This is not an allergic reaction. Naloxone itself is not allergenic; the symptoms are opioid withdrawal precipitated by naloxone's antagonism. Antihistamines will not help.
❌ Incorrect. The patient IS reversed (RR 14, alert). More naloxone will not improve symptoms; it will worsen withdrawal. The symptoms are predictable withdrawal, not inadequate reversal.
❌ Incorrect. There is no evidence of stimulant intoxication. The constellation of myalgias, cramping, dysphoria within 15 minutes of naloxone is consistent with acute opioid withdrawal, not stimulant effects.
✅ Correct. This is textbook acute opioid withdrawal induced by naloxone. Symptoms are very uncomfortable but not life-threatening. This emphasizes the importance of low-dose, incremental naloxone dosing (starting 0.04 mg in chronic users) to minimize withdrawal while still reversing dangerous respiratory depression.
Q4. A 45-year-old male on long-term buprenorphine therapy for opioid use disorder accidentally ingests naloxone 2 mg from a bystander naloxone kit after opioid intoxication by co-ingestants. He develops severe acute withdrawal symptoms within 20 minutes. Why does buprenorphine differ from other opioids in this regard?
  • A. Buprenorphine is a full agonist like morphine; naloxone has standard antagonist affinity and readily displaces it
  • B. Buprenorphine is rapidly metabolized to more potent opioid metabolites; naloxone cannot block these active metabolites
  • C. Buprenorphine has HIGH AFFINITY for and SLOW DISSOCIATION from μ-receptors; high-dose naloxone (2 mg) can competitively displace it, causing acute withdrawal
  • D. Buprenorphine is not metabolized by the liver; naloxone cannot access CNS-bound buprenorphine
❌ Incorrect. Buprenorphine is a PARTIAL agonist, not a full agonist. Its high receptor affinity and slow dissociation make naloxone displacement difficult at standard doses.
❌ Incorrect. Buprenorphine's toxicity is from the parent compound, not active metabolites. The issue is its receptor pharmacodynamics (high affinity, slow dissociation), not metabolism.
✅ Correct. Buprenorphine's partial agonist activity and unique receptor binding characteristics (high affinity, slow dissociation) make it difficult for standard naloxone doses to displace. High-dose naloxone (2 mg IV) can competitively overcome this, but standard doses (0.4 mg) often fail to fully reverse buprenorphine effects.
❌ Incorrect. Buprenorphine IS metabolized (though not hepatically); the issue is not bioavailability but receptor binding kinetics.

Thai EM Board — InTraining Exam MCQs

Q1. A 19-year-old college student is brought to the ED after being found unresponsive following use of a substance at a party. Physical examination reveals: RR 8 breaths/min, BP 88/56 mmHg, HR 48 bpm, pinpoint pupils, no response to pain, clear lung fields bilaterally. Which of the following is the most efficient approach to simultaneously manage airway compromise and treat the presumed underlying condition?
  • A. Intubate immediately; naloxone can be administered post-intubation if opioid toxicity is confirmed
  • B. Initiate bag-valve-mask ventilation, administer naloxone 2 mg IV, continue supportive care pending response
  • C. Administer naloxone 0.04 mg IV and observe for response before deciding on airway management
  • D. Attempt central venous access and administer dopamine infusion for hypotension; reassess airway once perfusion is improved
❌ Incorrect. Intubation is time-consuming and invasive when naloxone may reverse the underlying condition within minutes. Intubation should be reserved for cases not responding to naloxone or when acute lung injury is present.
✅ Correct. This approach provides immediate oxygenation while attempting pharmacologic reversal. If naloxone works (respiratory rate improves within 1-2 min), intubation is avoided. This is the standard approach per Tintinalli: 'Airway protection and ventilatory assistance are the most important treatment steps; use bag-valve-mask as needed to maintain adequate oxygenation and ventilation. After adequate ventilation is ensured, administer naloxone.'
❌ Incorrect. While 0.04 mg is appropriate for chronic opioid users, this patient is apneic and critically ill. Low-dose naloxone will not reverse apnea/cyanosis. High-dose naloxone (2 mg) is indicated regardless of opioid use history in this scenario.
❌ Incorrect. Vasopressors are not indicated as first-line in opioid-induced hypotension. Hypotension usually resolves with reversal of respiratory depression (improved oxygenation) and correction of acidosis. Naloxone is the treatment of choice; vasopressors are adjunctive only if hypotension persists despite naloxone.
Q2. A 55-year-old male with uncontrolled chronic pain was prescribed methadone 20 mg daily. After 5 days of therapy, he is brought to the ED lethargic with RR 6, pupils pinpoint, and heart rate 42 bpm. He is given naloxone 2 mg IV, which initially improves his respiratory rate to 16 and mental status. However, at 90 minutes, his respiratory rate drops to 8 again. Which pharmacokinetic property of methadone accounts for this re-sedation?
  • A. Methadone has poor oral bioavailability; only 10-20% reaches systemic circulation and lasts 3-4 hours
  • B. Methadone is rapidly metabolized to active metabolites with longer duration than the parent drug
  • C. Methadone has a long half-life (12-18 hours or up to 59 hours with chronic dosing) and extended duration of action (initially 8-12 hours, extending to 22-36 hours); naloxone's duration is only 20-90 minutes. Thus, naloxone wears off before methadone's effect ends, causing re-sedation.
  • D. Methadone displaces naloxone from μ-opioid receptors due to its higher receptor affinity
❌ Incorrect. While methadone does undergo first-pass metabolism, it has GOOD oral bioavailability (about 40-99% for methadone specifically). Its duration of action is 8-12 hours initially and extends to 22-36 hours with chronic dosing, not 3-4 hours.
❌ Incorrect. While methadone is hepatically metabolized, the issue is not active metabolites but rather the long half-life of methadone itself (12-18 hours initially, up to 59 hours with chronic dosing).
✅ Correct. This is the fundamental pharmacokinetic mismatch. Methadone's prolonged effect outlasts naloxone's duration, necessitating continuous infusion of naloxone, not repeated boluses. This is why the textbook states: 'This is especially true for certain long-acting opioids, such as buprenorphine and methadone; for exposures to sustained-release preparations... A continuous infusion should be considered only if the patient responded to the initial naloxone bolus and subsequently required repeat administration.'
❌ Incorrect. While methadone does have affinity for μ-receptors, naloxone is a competitive antagonist that can displace agonists. The issue is not receptor affinity but rather the duration mismatch.
Q3. A 26-year-old female on buprenorphine maintenance therapy for opioid use disorder presents with acute opioid intoxication from an unknown co-ingestant (presumed heroin). She has RR 6, altered mental status, and miosis. Standard naloxone 0.4 mg IV is administered. Her respiratory depression does NOT improve; RR remains 6 and mental status worsens. What is the most appropriate next step?
  • A. Discontinue naloxone; it may precipitate severe withdrawal in this buprenorphine-maintained patient
  • B. Administer activated charcoal to slow absorption of the co-ingestant opioid
  • C. Intubate for airway protection and mechanically ventilate; avoid additional naloxone
  • D. Administer HIGH-DOSE naloxone 2 mg IV immediately; this may overcome buprenorphine's high receptor affinity and dissociation kinetics, and help reverse co-ingestant heroin as well
❌ Incorrect. While naloxone can precipitate withdrawal in buprenorphine-maintained patients, the patient is currently apneic and in respiratory distress. Life-threatening respiratory depression takes priority over withdrawal symptoms. Naloxone must be given; dose should be adjusted, not avoided.
❌ Incorrect. Activated charcoal is minimally helpful for opioids and does nothing to reverse already-absorbed heroin. This is not the acute treatment of apnea.
❌ Incorrect. Intubation may be necessary eventually, but naloxone should not be withheld. High-dose naloxone should be attempted first because buprenorphine's receptor characteristics may require higher doses. This patient may respond to 2 mg naloxone IV, avoiding intubation.
✅ Correct. Buprenorphine's unique pharmacodynamics (high affinity, slow dissociation) mean standard naloxone doses are often ineffective. High-dose naloxone (2 mg) can competitively displace buprenorphine from the μ-receptor and also reverse the co-ingestant heroin. If 2 mg is inadequate, repeat dosing or naloxone infusion may be needed. The point is: do NOT avoid naloxone in buprenorphine-maintained patients; instead, use HIGHER doses.

McGraw-Hill Specialty Board Review MCQs

Q1. A 34-year-old presents with somnolence, miosis, and RR of 8. She admits to taking 'too many pain pills.' She responds to sternal rub and follows commands. Pulse oximetry is 92% on room air. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
  • A. Immediate orotracheal intubation for airway protection
  • B. Supplemental oxygen followed by IV naloxone
  • C. IV fluids and activated charcoal
  • D. Urine drug screen and await results before treatment
Supplemental oxygen is the first step — SpO2 92% indicates hypoxemia that should be corrected immediately. Naloxone should then be given to reverse respiratory depression. Bag-valve-mask is not yet needed as she is maintaining her airway. Intubation is not indicated for a responsive patient.
Q2. Which of the following is a TRUE statement regarding naloxone pharmacokinetics and dosing?
  • A. Naloxone has a longer half-life than morphine
  • B. A single IV dose of naloxone will reliably reverse all opioid overdoses for 4-6 hours
  • C. Re-narcotization occurs when naloxone's duration of action is shorter than the opioid's
  • D. Intranasal naloxone provides faster onset than IV naloxone
Naloxone has a shorter half-life (30-90 minutes) than most opioids it reverses. This creates risk of re-narcotization — the opioid effect returns as naloxone wears off. This is the key reason why observation after reversal is essential, and why naloxone infusions are used for long-acting opioid overdoses.
Q3. A 45-year-old male presents with altered mental status and pinpoint pupils after ingesting 'something from the medicine cabinet.' He is bradycardic (HR 44) and hypotensive (BP 80/50). This presentation most suggests ingestion of which specific opioid?
  • A. Codeine
  • B. Hydrocodone
  • C. Tramadol
  • D. Methadone
Methadone is uniquely associated with significant QTc prolongation and cardiac toxicity, including bradycardia and hypotension beyond typical opioid effects. Methadone also has a very long half-life (24-36h) and can cause Torsades de Pointes. The combination of severe cardiovascular depression with opioid toxidrome should raise suspicion for methadone.
Q4. A 29-year-old with opioid use disorder on buprenorphine/naloxone maintenance is brought in after using heroin in an attempt to 'get high.' She complains of severe withdrawal symptoms and is requesting IV opioids for pain. Why is achieving opioid effect with standard IV opioids particularly difficult in this patient?
  • A. Buprenorphine's high receptor affinity blocks full agonist binding, requiring exceptionally high opioid doses
  • B. The naloxone component of buprenorphine/naloxone binds irreversibly to opioid receptors
  • C. Opioid use disorder permanently reduces the number of mu-opioid receptors
  • D. Heroin use simultaneously activates kappa receptors that antagonize mu-receptor effects
Buprenorphine is a partial mu-agonist with very high receptor affinity and a 'ceiling effect.' It competitively occupies mu-receptors and blocks full agonists. For full opioid agonists to displace buprenorphine and achieve effect, extremely high doses are required — doses that risk respiratory depression even in tolerant patients. This is why buprenorphine is effective for maintenance (blocks euphoria from opioid use) and why breakthrough analgesia in buprenorphine patients requires specialized approaches.

End-of-Chapter Assessment: 20 Questions

Q1. Which opioid receptor, when stimulated, produces euphoria, analgesia, and respiratory depression?
  • A. μ (mu)-receptor
  • B. κ (kappa)-receptor
  • C. δ (delta)-receptor
  • D. All three receptors equally
✅ Correct.
❌ Incorrect. Kappa-receptor produces dysphoria, not euphoria.
❌ Incorrect. Delta-receptor has minor analgesia and antidepressant effects, not euphoria or respiratory depression.
❌ Incorrect. While all opioids have μ-activity, kappa and delta effects vary by drug.
Q2. Which of the following opioids has high oral bioavailability and can be given PO with reasonable effect?
  • A. Morphine (standard tablets)
  • B. Oxycodone
  • C. Heroin
  • D. Fentanyl (tablets, not transdermal)
❌ Incorrect. Morphine has poor oral bioavailability (~25%) due to first-pass metabolism.
✅ Correct. Oxycodone has excellent oral bioavailability (~60-87%).
❌ Incorrect. Heroin has very poor oral bioavailability; it is typically injected or inhaled.
❌ Incorrect. Fentanyl has very poor oral bioavailability; sublingual/buccal formulations exist (lozenges, transdermal) but regular tablets are not effective.
Q3. A patient presents with RR 6, miosis, lethargy, and urine drug screen positive for opioids. You are concerned about non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Which finding on chest radiograph would support this diagnosis?
  • A. Bilateral infiltrates with enlarged cardiac silhouette (cardiomegaly)
  • B. Unilateral infiltrate with pleural effusion
  • C. Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with normal cardiac silhouette
  • D. Clear lung fields; pulmonary edema ruled out
❌ Incorrect. This suggests cardiogenic pulmonary edema, not opioid-induced acute lung injury.
❌ Incorrect. Unilateral infiltrates suggest pneumonia or aspiration, not noncardiogenic pulmonary edema from opioid toxicity.
✅ Correct. This is the classic finding of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, pathognomonic for opioid-induced acute lung injury.
❌ Incorrect. Clear lung fields do not rule out acute lung injury, which can occur immediately or be delayed up to 24 hours after overdose.
Q4. Tramadol overdose is associated with which serious complication that is NOT reversed by naloxone?
  • A. Respiratory depression (reversed by naloxone)
  • B. Seizures (NOT reversed by naloxone)
  • C. Miosis (pinpoint pupils, reversed by naloxone)
  • D. Nausea and vomiting (reversed by antiemetics)
❌ Incorrect. While respiratory depression can occur at high tramadol doses, it IS reversed by naloxone.
✅ Correct. Tramadol-induced seizures are from serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake effects, not μ-opioid activity.
❌ Incorrect. Miosis from tramadol's μ-opioid activity is reversible by naloxone.
❌ Incorrect. Nausea is a common opioid effect but is addressed with antiemetics, not naloxone.
Q5. Which statement accurately describes the relationship between naloxone half-life and its duration of action in opioid overdose?
  • A. Naloxone half-life is 60-90 minutes, so its effect lasts 60-90 minutes regardless of opioid amount
  • B. Naloxone half-life is 20 minutes; its effect lasts approximately 20 minutes in all cases
  • C. Naloxone's duration of action always exceeds its half-life, so re-sedation is rare
  • D. Naloxone half-life is 60-90 minutes, but duration of action can be as short as 20 minutes with large opioid agonist present, explaining re-sedation risk
❌ Incorrect. Duration of action can be as short as 20 minutes with large opioid amounts, much shorter than the half-life.
❌ Incorrect. Half-life is 60-90 minutes; duration of action varies 20-90 minutes depending on opioid amount.
❌ Incorrect. Duration of action is usually SHORTER than half-life due to large opioid agonist amounts.
✅ Correct. This pharmacokinetic mismatch is the key to understanding re-sedation and the need for naloxone infusions.
Q6. A 56-year-old man on long-term methadone maintenance therapy for chronic pain presents with altered mental status and RR 8. ECG shows QTc interval of 520 milliseconds. What is the recommended management regarding methadone dosage?
  • A. No dosage adjustment needed; all QT prolongation from methadone is benign
  • B. Acute overdose requires naloxone infusion and supportive care; after stabilization, consider methadone dose reduction given QTc >500 milliseconds
  • C. Immediately discontinue methadone; switch to alternative analgesic
  • D. Administer magnesium and potassium; no dosage change needed
❌ Incorrect. QTc >500 milliseconds indicates significant prolongation with risk of torsades de pointes and requires dose reduction consideration.
✅ Correct. Acute management is standard opioid OD treatment. Chronic management of QT >500 involves dose reduction/discontinuation per Tintinalli: 'Patients who develop a QTc interval of >500 milliseconds should be considered for methadone dosage reduction or discontinuation.'
❌ Incorrect. While dose reduction is considered, abrupt discontinuation of chronic methadone risks severe withdrawal. This should be done gradually under careful monitoring.
❌ Incorrect. While electrolyte repletion is important, QTc >500 indicates need for dose reduction consideration, not just electrolyte management.
Q7. How does buprenorphine's partial agonist activity affect its overdose toxicity profile compared to full μ-agonist opioids like heroin?
  • A. Buprenorphine causes more severe respiratory depression than heroin due to higher receptor affinity
  • B. Buprenorphine causes identical respiratory depression as heroin; toxicity profiles are the same
  • C. Buprenorphine's partial agonist activity causes respiratory depression to plateau at higher doses (ceiling effect), whereas full agonists show escalating respiratory depression; however, buprenorphine's high receptor affinity makes naloxone reversal difficult
  • D. Buprenorphine causes no respiratory depression due to its partial agonist activity
❌ Incorrect. While buprenorphine has high receptor affinity, it is a partial agonist with PLATEAU effect, so respiratory depression is less severe than full agonists.
❌ Incorrect. Buprenorphine's partial agonist activity creates a plateau effect, limiting respiratory depression severity compared to heroin's escalating dose-response.
✅ Correct. This is the unique dual nature of buprenorphine toxicity: plateau of respiratory depression (good) but difficult naloxone reversal due to pharmacodynamic properties (bad).
❌ Incorrect. Buprenorphine DOES cause respiratory depression; it just plateaus rather than escalating infinitely. It is still dangerous in overdose.
Q8. A 48-year-old with severe liver disease chronically abuses heroin. His codeine elimination is slower than expected for his age. Which cytochrome P450 enzyme is most likely impaired?
  • A. CYP1A2
  • B. CYP2D6
  • C. CYP3A4
  • D. CYP2C9
❌ Incorrect. CYP1A2 is important for other drugs (theophylline, caffeine), not primarily codeine.
✅ Correct. Codeine is primarily metabolized to morphine via CYP2D6.
❌ Incorrect. While CYP3A4 is involved in methadone metabolism, CYP2D6 is primary for codeine.
❌ Incorrect. CYP2C9 is important for warfarin and NSAIDs, not codeine.
Q9. Which finding is most specific for distinguishing opioid-induced miosis from miosis caused by other toxins?
  • A. Miosis alone is specific for opioid intoxication
  • B. Miosis with bradycardia is pathognomonic for opioids
  • C. Rapid response to naloxone distinguishes opioid miosis from others (but requires giving naloxone)
  • D. The TRIAD of miosis + respiratory depression + altered mental status is highly specific for opioid intoxication; additional features like hypothermia strengthen the diagnosis
❌ Incorrect. Miosis occurs with cholinergic toxins, antipsychotics, and others.
❌ Incorrect. While common, bradycardia + miosis can occur with clonidine and others.
❌ Partially correct but not the most practical answer (requires drug administration for diagnosis).
✅ Correct. The classic toxidrome (miosis, lethargy, respiratory depression) is much more specific than any single finding. This pattern + circumstantial evidence (drug paraphernalia, needle marks) makes clinical diagnosis highly sensitive.
Q10. A 3-year-old ingests a single diphenoxylate/atropine tablet. What is the FIRST clinical syndrome expected?
  • A. Anticholinergic toxidrome (dry mouth, mydriasis, urinary retention, tachycardia)
  • B. Opioid toxidrome (miosis, respiratory depression, lethargy)
  • C. Both anticholinergic and opioid toxidromes simultaneously
  • D. Cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE, fasciculations)
✅ Correct. Atropine dominates initially; opioid effects follow later.
❌ Incorrect. This is the SECOND phase, occurring after 6-12 hours.
❌ Incorrect. They occur sequentially, not simultaneously.
❌ Incorrect. Atropine is an ANTICHOLINERGIC (opposite of cholinergic).
Q11. A patient requires a naloxone infusion after buprenorphine overdose. When calculating the infusion rate, what formula is used?
  • A. Full wake-up dose per hour
  • B. Two-thirds of the wake-up dose per hour
  • C. Half the wake-up dose per hour
  • D. Wake-up dose divided by the patient's weight in kg per hour
❌ Incorrect. This would lead to excessive naloxone dosing; two-thirds is the standard.
✅ Correct. This is the standard Tintinalli recommendation.
❌ Incorrect. Two-thirds is the standard, not one-half.
❌ Incorrect. The formula is two-thirds of the wake-up dose, not weight-adjusted.
Q12. Which is the primary advantage of intranasal naloxone over IV naloxone in the prehospital setting?
  • A. Intranasal naloxone has faster onset than IV naloxone
  • B. Intranasal naloxone lasts longer than IV naloxone
  • C. Intranasal naloxone is non-invasive, safe for bystander administration, and avoids needlestick risk while providing effective reversal
  • D. Intranasal naloxone has better bioavailability than IV in all patients
❌ Incorrect. IV is faster (1-2 min vs 6-8 min).
❌ Incorrect. Duration is similar (20-90 min for both).
✅ Correct. This is why intranasal naloxone is used in bystander programs and by EMS.
❌ Incorrect. IV has complete bioavailability; intranasal is less reliable.
Q13. A patient with opioid use disorder is prescribed buprenorphine for medication-assisted treatment (MAT) in the ED. When is the EARLIEST timing to safely initiate buprenorphine?
  • A. Immediately upon arrival, concurrent with naloxone if needed
  • B. After the acute opioid intoxication is resolved and the patient enters early withdrawal (6-12+ hours), assessed using Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale
  • C. Buprenorphine should never be started in the ED; this must be done in an outpatient opioid treatment program
  • D. Only after the patient has been in withdrawal for 3+ days (peak withdrawal)
❌ Incorrect. Giving buprenorphine to an actively intoxicated patient (or just after naloxone) will precipitate severe withdrawal.
✅ Correct. Buprenorphine is initiated once the patient is in early-to-moderate withdrawal, assessed by COWS score.
❌ Incorrect. Tintinalli explicitly states buprenorphine can be used in the ED for withdrawal and be prescribed upon discharge.
❌ Incorrect. This would be unnecessary; early withdrawal is sufficient. Waiting for peak withdrawal would cause excessive suffering.
Q14. A 62-year-old heroin user with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) is on chronic methadone maintenance. His methadone blood level is lower than expected. Which medication is MOST LIKELY causing this interaction?
  • A. Fluconazole (antifungal)
  • B. Omeprazole (proton pump inhibitor)
  • C. Protease inhibitor or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (component of ART)
  • D. Clarithromycin (macrolide)
❌ Incorrect. Fluconazole INCREASES methadone levels (inhibits metabolism).
❌ Incorrect. Omeprazole INCREASES methadone levels.
✅ Correct. Many ART drugs INDUCE methadone metabolism, lowering levels and potentially precipitating withdrawal.
❌ Incorrect. Clarithromycin PRECIPITATES withdrawal, but by a different mechanism (enzyme induction); protease inhibitors are more directly causative of lowered levels.
Q15. Which body-packer presentation requires the HIGHEST naloxone doses and prolonged infusion?
  • A. Body-packer with ruptured heroin packet causing severe, prolonged toxicity
  • B. Standard heroin injection in a chronic user with mild respiratory depression
  • C. Fentanyl patch overdose in an opioid-naive patient
  • D. Methadone maintenance patient taking an extra dose of prescribed methadone
✅ Correct. Ruptured packets release massive opioid amounts, requiring large sustained naloxone doses and infusions.
❌ Incorrect. This requires standard naloxone dosing, not high-dose prolonged infusion.
❌ Incorrect. While fentanyl is potent, a ruptured body-packer is typically MORE severe due to the large amount.
❌ Incorrect. This is significant but less severe than a ruptured body-packer.
Q16. Why is increased monitoring of serum electrolytes important in acute methadone overdose?
  • A. Hyperkalemia is a direct toxic effect of methadone
  • B. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia increase risk of torsades de pointes and other dysrhythmias in the context of QT prolongation
  • C. Methadone causes rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria, requiring fluid management
  • D. Electrolyte abnormalities are unrelated to methadone toxicity
❌ Incorrect. Methadone does not directly cause hyperkalemia; rather, electrolyte abnormalities worsen QT prolongation.
✅ Correct. Methadone-induced QT prolongation is worsened by electrolyte deficiencies; repletion is essential.
❌ Incorrect. While rhabdomyolysis can occur with some opioid overdoses, electrolyte monitoring in methadone OD is primarily for QT management.
❌ Incorrect. They significantly impact cardiac arrhythmia risk in methadone QT prolongation.
Q17. A patient presenting with the classic opioid triad has respiratory depression unresponsive to bag-valve-mask ventilation and initial naloxone 2 mg IV. What is the MOST appropriate next step after repeating the naloxone dose?
  • A. Continue bag-valve-mask ventilation indefinitely; intubation is not indicated
  • B. Administer high-dose IV flumazenil to reverse possible benzodiazepine co-ingestant
  • C. Give another naloxone dose immediately and transport to ICU without securing airway
  • D. Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation (possibly after additional naloxone bolus), especially if acute lung injury is suspected
❌ Incorrect. Prolonged bag-valve-mask is exhausting and unreliable; intubation should be considered early if naloxone is ineffective.
❌ Incorrect. Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdoses and carries seizure risk; it is not indicated here.
❌ Incorrect. Repeated naloxone may be needed, but if unresponsive, airway management should not be delayed.
✅ Correct. This provides definitive airway protection, easy suctioning, and alternative medication routes. It is indicated if naloxone is ineffective.
Q18. A patient on long-term oral morphine for cancer pain presents after acute overdose. His current Glasgow Coma Scale is 9, RR 10, SpO2 88% on RA. After initial airway management and 0.4 mg IV naloxone, he wakes but is combative and demands to leave. What is the most important next step?
  • A. Discharge with prescription for oral naltrexone and 24-hour follow-up
  • B. Repeat naloxone 0.4 mg IV every 30 minutes for 2 hours then discharge
  • C. Observe for at least 4-6 hours; start naloxone infusion if re-narcotization occurs
  • D. Admit to ICU for 24-hour intubation regardless of current mental status
❌ Incorrect. Naltrexone is for maintenance therapy, not acute overdose. Discharging after short-acting opioid reversal risks re-narcotization after naloxone wears off.
❌ Incorrect. Repeated boluses are not sufficient monitoring. A naloxone infusion is more appropriate if needed, and observation must continue for the duration of risk.
✅ Correct. Re-narcotization occurs when naloxone wears off before the opioid is cleared. Morphine's duration exceeds naloxone's, requiring extended observation. A naloxone infusion (2/3 of reversal dose/hour) manages re-narcotization.
❌ Incorrect. If the patient is responsive and protecting their airway after reversal, intubation is not indicated. Observation with naloxone infusion readiness is appropriate.
Q19. A 22-year-old woman accidentally ingests her partner's 100-mcg fentanyl transdermal patch. She presents obtunded with RR 8 and SpO2 84%. Which statement BEST describes the expected clinical course and naloxone requirements?
  • A. Single naloxone bolus will provide adequate reversal; observe 2 hours and discharge
  • B. Prolonged naloxone infusion and ICU admission are required due to large drug reservoir in the patch
  • C. Fentanyl's lipophilicity prevents significant oral absorption
  • D. Whole bowel irrigation is contraindicated due to risk of accelerating patch absorption
❌ Incorrect. Fentanyl patch ingestion provides a sustained drug reservoir. Single-dose naloxone will wear off well before fentanyl is cleared, leading to re-narcotization.
✅ Correct. Patches contain up to 1-2 mg fentanyl. Ingestion causes large bioavailable dose with prolonged absorption, requiring naloxone infusions for up to 24 hours. ICU monitoring is essential.
❌ Incorrect. While fentanyl is lipophilic and highly protein-bound, oral ingestion of a patch provides a massive dose that is absorbed through GI mucosa. Life-threatening toxicity occurs.
❌ Incorrect. WBI (with polyethylene glycol) is appropriate to remove the patch from the GI tract and reduce ongoing absorption. It does not significantly accelerate absorption.
Q20. A body-packer is brought by police after arrest. Plain abdominal X-ray shows multiple rounded opacities consistent with drug packets. The patient is currently asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
  • A. Immediate emergency laparotomy to manually remove all packets
  • B. Administer naloxone prophylactically to prevent toxicity from potential packet rupture
  • C. Upper endoscopy to retrieve packets from the stomach under direct visualization
  • D. Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol solution; monitor until all packets passed
❌ Incorrect. Surgery (laparotomy) is reserved for symptomatic patients with bowel obstruction or failed non-surgical management. Asymptomatic patients should first receive WBI.
❌ Incorrect. Prophylactic naloxone is not standard for asymptomatic patients. Naloxone should be immediately available but given only when opioid toxicity manifests.
❌ Incorrect. Endoscopy risks packet rupture during retrieval. It may be considered for gastric packets if identified early, but is not the first-line approach. WBI is preferred for asymptomatic patients.
✅ Correct. WBI is the standard non-surgical approach for asymptomatic body-packers. It accelerates GI transit to remove packets before rupture. All patients require close monitoring with naloxone available.
